newsitem.title: USA: Mexico drugs issue goes down to wire.
newsitem.headline: Mexico drugs issue goes down to wire.

text.p: Negotiations on draft legislation calling on Mexico to crack down on illegal drugs went down to the wire on Wednesday as the Clinton administration was reported to have balked at a compromise offer by key senators.

At a news conference the senators warned the administration that failure to reach an accord would lead to a rancorous Senate debate and vote on a measure to overturn President Bill Clinton's finding that Mexico is fully cooperating in the anti-drug war.

Republicans Paul Coverdell of Georgia and Kay Bailey Hutchison of Texas and Democrat Dianne Feinstein of California unveiled what Coverdell called "very reasonable" legislation that stops well short of "decertification" of Mexico.
Coverdell said the administration's sticking point was its objection to giving Congress any role in assessing the adequacy of anti-drug measures by Mexico and the United States.
"I think we're at a bit of an impasse here," Hutchison said.

Coverdell said intense discussions were continuing and predicted the issue would be settled one way or another on Thursday. Without a compromise, the Senate would be forced to debate a decertification resolution and vote on it. Feinstein predicted it would not approve unvarnished decertification.

The three senators and others have been in negotiations with high administration officials including Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin since last Thursday after the House voted to decertify Mexico but give it 90 days to improve its anti-drug performance.
The action drew a sharp response from Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo who said his country's dignity and sovereignty were not negotiable.

The Senate negotiators emphasised that they were going the last mile to accommodate administration concerns. The draft legislation leaves in place Clinton's Feb. 28 certification of Mexico as a reliable anti-drug ally and delays the congressional response to drug-war reforms until Septemember, well after Clinton's April visit to Mexico and Mexican elections in July.

At that point Congress would be able to enact a resolution saying if implementation of reforms was adequate, but not to decertify Mexico. The proposed compromise states that Congress believes "that there has been ineffective and insufficient progress in halting the production in and transit through Mexico of illegal drugs."
It calls for a series of reforms including strengthening of U.S.-Mexican cooperation and bilateral border enforcement, implementation of money laundering laws and eradication of narcotics crops.
